ranked.name: One Square Meter
ranked.oneLiner: Point your phone at any small corner of chaos (a desk, a fridge shelf, a drawer, a dying plant). Claude turns that exact photo into a 7-minute rescue mission, then checks your after photo and gives you a satisfying before/after reveal.

ranked.name: Kiln
ranked.oneLiner: A pocket operating system that builds its own apps out of your real inbox and Drive. Each time you open it, new tiny tools have been made for problems you hadn't gotten around to naming.

ranked.name: Underlay
ranked.oneLiner: Photograph any piece of your life (a receipt, the fridge, your closet, a utility bill, a pill bottle) and it turns into a living, scrubbable model of the invisible system behind it. You drag the numbers and watch your future change.

ranked.name: Correspondence
ranked.oneLiner: A quiet place for tending the people in your life: it notices who you've drifted from in your real email history and helps you write them one sincere letter, in your own voice, in about two minutes.

ranked.name: Clearing
ranked.oneLiner: The page reads your real inbox and Drive and shows you one thing at a time: a single decision only you can make, already prepared, which you settle with one deliberate gesture.

ranked.name: Loose Threads
ranked.oneLiner: An inbox-powered relationship mender: each session it finds people you've drifted from or left unanswered, tells you where you left off with them, and helps you write a message that only you could send. Then it tells you you're done.

ranked.name: The Council of Former Selves
ranked.oneLiner: Your old Drive documents and emails come back as a round table of past versions of you, who remember what you've forgotten and help you decide what to do next, with citations.

ranked.name: Patina
ranked.oneLiner: Photograph the things you own and the app quietly builds a museum of your physical life, finding each object's receipt, warranty, value, care and story in your own email.

ranked.name: Dig
ranked.oneLiner: A daily treasure hunt through your own life for money you're losing. It digs your receipts, subscriptions and refund windows out of Gmail, and prices the stuff in your photos. Every find goes into a 'found money' vault with a dollar total.

ranked.name: Tidepool
ranked.oneLiner: Your real Gmail inbox as a physical tide pool. Every thread is a creature with mass, temperature, and age. You clear your life by sculpting replies with your hands, not by typing.

ranked.name: Unclaimed
ranked.oneLiner: A treasure hunt through your own inbox and Drive for money, time and promises you're leaving on the table: forgotten subscriptions, refunds you never chased, warranties about to lapse, forms half-filled. Claude prepares the fix for each one so you just approve.

ranked.name: Owed
ranked.oneLiner: A swipe deck of everything you owe other people, made from your real inbox. Each swipe settles one: Claude has already written the reply in your voice, and you approve it.

ranked.name: Futures Bench
ranked.oneLiner: A workbench where any real decision you're stuck on becomes a live simulation of your possible futures. Friends can join and put their thumbs on the same assumption knobs in real time.

ranked.name: Overflow
ranked.oneLiner: A falling-block puzzle game where the blocks are your real unanswered emails, forgotten docs and pending decisions, and every line you clear actually gets done.

ranked.name: Docket
ranked.oneLiner: A live court for real-life decisions. You file a dilemma, friends who open the link become the jury in real time, and Claude acts as the judge: it pulls evidence from your email and docs, cross-examines you, and issues a verdict written to Drive.

hybrids.name: Clearing
hybrids.combines: I1 Clearing (one prepared decision at a time, hold to commit, a natural end, the fog), I3/I10 Correspondence and Loose Threads (people you've drifted from, a letter in your voice, the 'they wrote back' reward), I11 One Square Meter (a photo of a physical corner becomes a short mission with pins and a before/after reveal), and I12 Unclaimed (money and deadlines left on the table, with the evidence shown).
hybrids.pitch: There is one surface, one card, and one gesture. Each card is a single loop in your life that only you can close, with the work already done. It might be a person ('Maya asked how the job was going, 14 months ago. A first line is waiting.'), an obligation ('Your boots' return window closes Thursday. The request is drafted.'), or your physical world ('Photograph your nightstand.' Claude returns three pins and a 6:00 timer, and the after photo wipes across the before). Every card speaks the same language: one sentence of context, the evidence behind it, one prepared action, and hold to commit, swipe to defer or tap to rephrase. Every action produces a Gmail draft, a Drive file or a real change in your room. Nothing is ever sent for you. Each closed loop thins the fog at the top of the screen. When today's loops are gone, the screen says 'Clear.' and stops. A short 'Since last time' line greets your return: 'Maya wrote back. $62 refunded. The nightstand held.' The rewards are real and come from outside the app, so nothing here has to be engineered to hook you. It's buildable as five pieces: (1) the Gmail/Drive agent and card schema, (2) the people and letters engine with a voice profile, (3) the photo mission with pins, timer and before/after, (4) the card stage, hold gesture and fog, (5) db memory, the 'since last time' check and demo mode.
hybrids.objection: About eight of these fifteen pitches are the same app: an agent that reads your inbox and drafts a reply for your approval. It appears as a tide pool, a Tetris well, a debt ledger, a kiln, a treasure dig and a bounty board. A new costume is not novelty, and a metaphor laid over a list is decoration, not design. Worse, almost every one of them depends on triage quality against an inbox nobody can test beforehand. If the first card misreads a newsletter as a friend or invents a $38 refund, trust is gone and no fog, physics or combo will win it back. The field should stop adding mechanics and spend its effort on making the first three cards precisely, quietly correct. It should also accept that an honest app ends: it replaces TikTok by being finished in four minutes, not by being endless.

hybrids.name: Dividend
hybrids.combines: I12 Unclaimed + I5 Dig (money found through inbox evidence), I10 Loose Threads (people owed, the capped daily hand, the replies-came-back reward) and I11 One Square Meter (photo missions with before/after reveals as the supply that never runs out), presented through I1 Clearing's one-prepared-card-at-a-time interface.
hybrids.pitch: Every session deals you today's hand of 5 prepared cards, each one a real return on two minutes of your thumb. There are three suits: Money (a subscription to cancel, a return window closing, a refund to claim, each with evidence and a ready Gmail draft), People (someone waiting on you, with a 'where you left off' recap and an opener in your voice) and Space (a one-photo mission: shoot a corner, get pinned steps and a 7-minute timer, then a before/after slider). One metric ties everything together: your Dividend, a running ledger of dollars recovered, people answered and square meters reclaimed. Each card shows its estimated value and how long it takes. Why open it tomorrow: the inbox suits refill honestly as mail arrives and deadlines get close, and on reopen you see 'Priya replied' and 'Refund landed: +$38 banked'. Because the Space suit never runs dry, the hand is never empty, which fixes the retention cliff every inbox-only concept has. The hand is capped at 5 (stop 'That's today.'), so it beats TikTok by ending with you richer. Build split for 5: (1) Gmail/Drive agent layer and card JSON schema, (2) the Money suit's detectors and claim drafts, (3) the People suit's ranking, recap and voice drafts, (4) the Space suit's vision missions, pins, timer and before/after, (5) the card-hand UI, ledger, db persistence and demo-mode data.
hybrids.objection: Ten of the fifteen pitches are the same product: an AI agent that reads Gmail and hands you prepared drafts, dressed as a constellation, a court, a tide pool, Tetris or a museum. Nearly all of them are built to end ('Clear.', 'That's today', 'debt-free'). That is ethical, but it quietly gives up on the brief. TikTok fills 30-60 minutes a day, and most of these fill 3 minutes, then run out of supply after the first week because inbox debt doesn't regrow fast enough to sustain a daily habit. Every one of them also bets the whole first session on an inbox nobody can test ahead of time. This user's address looks like a shop account, so it may be full of orders and suppliers rather than friends and refunds, and a thin first scan means no activation and no second visit. The winning concept needs one value metric, a source of supply that never runs out and doesn't depend on Gmail quality (the camera), and a real reason to come back tomorrow that isn't just 'more email arrived'.

hybrids.name: Workbench
hybrids.combines: I13 Kiln (self-forging tools from your Gmail/Drive and photos) + I7 Underlay (every tool is a live, scrubbable explorable model computed locally) + I11 One Square Meter (photo-in, physical action out, verified reveal) + I9's hinge (show which single assumption matters)
hybrids.pitch: Feed it your life (an inbox scan, a photo of the fridge, a bill, a receipt) and it forges small instruments rather than widgets. Each one is a live sentence with draggable numbers: 'You pay $87/mo across [6] subscriptions; cutting to [3] saves $412/yr.' Drag the 6 down and the cancellation drafts get prepared beside it as you go. 'Your fridge has [4] days before $23 of food turns; cook [this] tonight.' Here reading the tool, steering it and acting on it are the same gesture. The hinge variable in each instrument glows, and committing to a setting turns it into a real action: a Gmail draft, a Drive file, or a 7-minute photo mission that a later photo verifies. Later photos or new mail snap onto the existing instrument, with a ghost line showing where you said you'd be. Build split: (1) capture plus agentic forging over Gmail/Drive/images, (2) a declarative model schema with a sandboxed expression evaluator, (3) the scrubbable-prose and chart renderer, (4) the bench wall with db persistence and ghost-line history, (5) the action layer (drafts, files, photo missions with verification).
hybrids.objection: Ten of the fifteen pitches are the same app in different skins: an agent reads Gmail, writes a draft, and you approve or reject it on a card, a deck, a blob, a Tetris block or a star. Swapping the skin doesn't change the interaction. The person still accepts a pre-chewed output they can't see inside or steer, which is the passive, consume-the-feed posture the brief wants to escape. Almost nobody proposed a new medium where the person thinks with their hands and sees the structure behind their life. Two practical cracks sit underneath: every inbox concept assumes a rich personal Gmail (many people's inboxes are mostly receipts and newsletters), and every concept that proudly 'ends' gives a two-minute session that can't actually displace an hour of TikTok. The winner has to give the thumb something endlessly explorable and true, not a queue that runs dry.

hybrids.name: Tend
hybrids.combines: I1 Clearing (one prepared decision at a time, consent gesture, honest ending) + I3/I10 Correspondence/Loose Threads (one real person per day, drafts in your voice, real replies as the reward) + I11 One Square Meter (photo of a physical spot becomes a timed mission with before/after) + I7 Underlay's ghost line (come back to see whether reality followed your intention).
hybrids.pitch: A finite daily hand of three cards that each tend one part of your life: a Person (someone you left hanging, with the thread recap and a letter drafted in your voice), a Loop (one obligation or money leak from your inbox, already prepared: a reply, a cancellation, a warranty claim), and a Place (photograph one square meter of chaos and get a 7-minute pinned mission with a before/after reveal). Each card is fully prepared, and you finish it with a deliberate hold gesture. Gmail drafts only, nothing auto-sent. When all three are done the screen says 'Tended.' and stops, with no fourth card. The home screen is a single living picture, a garden or a lit window, that shows three real things: people warmed, loops closed, spaces reclaimed. It fills in with real replies ('Maya wrote back'). The Place card means it never depends on Gmail being rich, and the Person card means it never feels like admin. The pull is that every session leaves three true things better in your life, in under 10 minutes, and it is designed to end. Five clean build pieces: Gmail agent and card generators, the vision mission and before/after engine, the card deck and hold-gesture UI, the living home picture plus the reply check, and db persistence with demo fallback.
hybrids.objection: Nine of fifteen concepts are the same machine: an LLM agent reads Gmail and produces drafts, wrapped in different metaphors (fog, tide pool, Tetris, debt, treasure, kiln, constellation). A metaphor is not a new idea. Worse, they all rest on an unchecked assumption: that this person's Gmail holds their life. For a heavy TikTok user, real relationships live in iMessage, WhatsApp and Instagram DMs, which we cannot reach. Their inbox is mostly receipts, promotions and work. So the 'Maya, 214 days ago' magic moment may simply never happen, and the first session, the one that decides everything, may be 40 seconds of an agent spinner followed by a newsletter. Several pitches also chase 'addicting' through guilt (debt bars, sinking blobs, pressure from falling blocks) or slot-machine variable payouts. Those are the very mechanisms we are claiming to replace. A winner must be magical even on a thin inbox. That points toward the physical world, meaning the camera, as a guaranteed source of substance, and it must have a designed ending rather than an endless 'one more dig'.

hybrids.name: Kiln: a living desktop of explorable tools
hybrids.combines: Kiln (I13): generative tiles built from primitives, fusing and melting tiles. Underlay (I7): every tile is a scrubbable live model with draggable numbers and a ghost line. One Square Meter (I11) and Patina (I2): photos as a second source of reality alongside the inbox. Futures Bench (I9): the hinge, plus a drafted email that settles it. Clearing (I1) and Loose Threads (I10): one prepared action per tile, a draft by default, and a finite session.
hybrids.pitch: Each time you open it, Claude runs a timed tool loop over what changed in Gmail and Drive, plus any photo you drop into the kiln, and forges one to three new tools on your desktop. Claude never writes code; every tool is a declarative spec made from about 8 primitives. The key primitive comes from Underlay: a live sentence whose numbers you can drag. So the gym-membership receipt becomes 'You pay $49/mo and went ~2x/month, $24.50 a visit', and dragging the visits number reflows the cost per visit. A fridge photo becomes a spoil-by timeline. A lease email becomes a countdown with a scrubbable rent-increase scenario. Every tool shows its hinge, the one number that decides the answer, and offers one prepared real action: a Gmail draft, a label, a Drive file, or an .ics download, always confirmed and never sent automatically. Drag one tool onto another to fuse them (Packages plus Receipts becomes a Returns window tracker). Flick a tool into the fire to melt it, and Claude learns what you don't want. Press 'Commit' on a number and it becomes an intention; next week a ghost line shows where reality went compared with what you committed to. The session ends when today's new forgings have been seen and acted on, with a screen that says 'Kiln cooled. 3 tools forged, 2 loops closed.' The pull is authorship and surprise: you want to see what it made from your life today, and every copy is different. A split for 5 builders: (1) agent loop, Gmail/Drive tools, photo intake and the forge prompt with JSON validation and re-asking; (2) primitive renderer plus a sandboxed expression evaluator for the scrubbable prose and mini charts; (3) desktop shell, the forge and ember animation, fuse and melt gestures; (4) the action layer with confirmation sheets, drafts, labels, Drive files and .ics; (5) db persistence, intentions and ghost lines, negative preferences, and a demo desktop for use outside Claude.
hybrids.objection: Six of the 15 concepts (Clearing, Owed, Tidepool, Overflow, Loose Threads, Correspondence) are the same inbox-triage product in different skins: a card or a blob or a block, then a drafted reply, then done. Two more (Dig, Unclaimed) are the same money hunt. The field treats Gmail as the only reality and 'a finite deck of prepared actions' as the only interaction. That is a chore with a swipe gesture on it, and nobody craves chores at 11pm. Relief is not desire, so none of these will beat TikTok's pull. They are also being bet on an unchecked assumption: that this person's inbox holds rich personal and financial life. For most people it holds newsletters and receipts, while their real relationships live in text messages. The brief says 'something I could never have imagined', and the one thing that has only become possible in the last year is Claude generating software and models on the spot from your own world. Only a few concepts (Kiln, Underlay, Council) actually build on that. Everyone else used a frontier model as a very good email autocomplete.

debate:
Ives: Build I7, Underlay. It is the only finalist where the core gesture is new rather than a new costume on an old one.

First, what the others are. Five of the eight (H1, H2, H4, and much of H5 and I13) are the same object: an agent reads Gmail and lays a draft in front of you for approval. A fog, a garden, a card hand or a kiln on top of that is ornament. Ornament is what you add when the form has not been resolved. They also all depend on an inbox none of us can see. This person's address looks like a shop account, so it is probably full of orders, suppliers and promotions. A first session of 'Maya, 14 months ago' could just as easily be a spinner followed by a Shopify receipt. Whatever we build has to work even if Gmail returns nothing.

I13 Kiln is a dashboard. However it is presented, eight primitives give you eight kinds of widget, and 'Packages (4)' is a list with a glow on it. Fusing tiles is a demo trick. A dashboard is where attention goes to die quietly. H5 makes this worse by keeping every Kiln mechanic and adding Underlay, ghost lines, hinges, fuse, melt and a session ending. It is a feature list, and no one could hold it in their hand. H3 Workbench is the most serious hybrid, but it still has two sources of truth (inbox and camera) and two products (instruments and missions). Each costs the other its clarity.

I11 One Square Meter is the most humane design here and the one I respect most. It gets you off the screen, the timer screen has nothing to scroll, and the before/after reveal is earned. But it isn't something the person 'could never have imagined', because AI tidying coaches already exist. You can also only reset a nightstand so many times. It is a good tool, not a new medium.

Underlay is a new medium. You point the phone at an ordinary object and the object itself opens up, showing the system behind it, and you steer that system with your thumb. Reading it and changing it are the same gesture. There is no form, no submit button and no queue that runs dry. The camera is the supply: every receipt, shelf, bill, label and plant is a new door, and none of it depends on Gmail. The pull is honest. The reveal is a small piece of magic, scrubbing is a pleasure in the hand, and the ghost line is the most humane reason to return anyone proposed: you come back to see whether reality followed the future you chose. There are no streaks, chests or guilt.

The panel's objections are real, and they are design problems, not reasons to reject it. 'False precision' is fixed with honesty in the material, described below. 'A generic renderer is fragile' is fixed by restraint: one renderer, one sentence form, one small chart, nothing more. 'A party trick after the third receipt' is fixed by making the model persist and accumulate. The tenth fridge photo is more valuable than the first, because it lands on a model that already knows you.
  Improvements: 1. The photo is the interface. Do not render the model below the photo as a separate calculator. Draw it on the photo: hairlines from each line item, the fridge shelf or the bill's kWh figure to the live number it feeds. The object you photographed stays the hero, so you are touching your actual receipt, not a spreadsheet. That is the moment of 'I could never have imagined this'.

2. Truth is part of the material. Every number has one of two visual states. A solid number was read from your photo, and tapping it highlights the pixels it came from. A hollow, outlined number is an assumption Claude made, and it shows a small '?' until you set it yourself. You fill it in by dragging, and as you do the model becomes yours and becomes true. This removes the false-precision objection and turns calibrating the model into the core pleasure. Hard rule: no number without a source or an assumption marker, and no invented 'hours waiting' unless the user owns that variable.

3. One hinge per model, not a toolbox. Claude must name the single variable that changes the outcome most, and only that variable glows. One sentence, at most three live numbers, one small chart. If a model can't be said in one sentence, it isn't ready.

4. Models accumulate, so value compounds. Each new photo of the same kind snaps onto its existing model (all receipts, the fridge, the electric bill), so the atlas gets smarter instead of filling up with one-off calculators. Use a lookup_previous_model tool in the sample loop. The wall is a small set of living systems (Food, Energy, Things, Money, Plants), each with its ghost line, not a grid of 200 photos.

5. Every commit leads to the real world. Take one piece from I11: 'Commit' becomes a single concrete act. That might be a 7-minute pinned mission on that same photo (cook these three things tonight, before the $23 spoils), an .ics reminder, or a single Gmail draft (cancel, return, ask). The next photo verifies the act and moves the ghost line. Gmail is an optional output, never the required input.

6. A designed ending. Each session is one object, explored and committed, followed by a closing line: 'Fridge: on track. $41 kept from spoiling this month.' One value metric across the app, measured against your own committed intentions.

7. Engineering restraint for the five builders: (1) vision and agent forging with a strict JSON schema, validation and re-asking; (2) a safe expression evaluator (a tiny parser, no eval); (3) the overlay renderer for hairlines, draggable numbers and the hinge glow on the photo, where all the polish goes; (4) the atlas wall with db and assets persistence and ghost-line history; (5) commit actions (missions, verification, drafts, .ics) plus a fully working demo atlas for use outside Claude.
  Ranking: I7 > H3 > I11 > H4 > H1 > H5 > H2 > I13

Zhuo: Build H3, "Workbench". I judge every pitch with two questions: why would someone open this tomorrow, and what single number proves it helped them? Applied honestly, those questions knock out most of the field.

The card-hand hybrids (H1 Clearing, H2 Dividend, H4 Tend) have a broken first session. All three open on an inbox scan, and this person's address looks like a shop account. Their Gmail is most likely orders, suppliers and promotions, not a "Maya, 14 months ago" moment. The People suit then has nothing to deal, the Money suit has to guess at refunds, and a single invented $38 destroys trust before the habit loop even starts. Even when they work, they are still the passive posture the person asked to escape. A pre-chewed output arrives, you hold to approve it, and it is over in three minutes. Supply also falls off a cliff after week one, because inbox debt doesn't grow back fast enough. H2's fix is to staple One Square Meter on as a fourth suit, which admits the core loop can't sustain itself.

I13 Kiln has the right thesis (software forged from your life) but the wrong output. "Packages (4)" is a dashboard tile, and dashboards are where retention curves go to die. Fusing tiles is a demo trick, not a job to be done.

I11 One Square Meter has the best activation in the field: one photo, value in seconds, and supply that never runs out. But it is the "cool, not groundbreaking" trap the person just rejected. AI cleaning coaches already exist, and you can only tidy a nightstand so many times.

I7 Underlay is the only truly new medium, but on its own it is a calculator with no action at the end. Once you've scrubbed a receipt three times, nothing in your life has changed.

H5 is the right blend, but it inherits Kiln's desktop, fusion, melting and forge theatrics. It is the biggest scope in the field for the smallest gain in retention.

H3 is the one concept where every part earns its place in the loop:
- Activation: a photo, which works on any inbox, including an empty one. It produces a live sentence with numbers you can drag, and that reveal is a moment people will screenshot.
- Engagement: the thumb does the thinking. You steer your own future instead of consuming a feed, and that directly answers the brief's "does something FOR me".
- Action: committing to a value produces real output, either a Gmail draft, a Drive file, or a 7-minute photo mission that an after photo verifies. That carries over I11's best part.
- Retention: the ghost line. You come back tomorrow because you made a promise to a curve, and the next photo or the next email shows whether reality followed. That is a reason to return built on your own intention rather than on guilt or a slot machine.
- One metric: commitments kept and verified, meaning a ghost line that reality actually matched.

It also suits a shop owner unusually well. Supplier invoices, order confirmations and shelf photos all become instruments for margin, reorder timing and stock spoilage, which is exactly where the inbox-as-friends concepts fail.

The real risk is false precision and a generic renderer that is fragile. Those are engineering problems, and they can be solved by constraining the system, which my improvements below do.
  Improvements: 1) Make the camera the front door and treat Gmail as the second act. The first session needs zero permissions: photo in, instrument out, in under 6 seconds. The "Can I look around your inbox?" prompt only appears after the first instrument has delighted the person, and the inbox then enriches the instruments that already exist (for example, "I found 5 more of these receipts, so your 3x/week is really 4.2x").

2) Make honesty visible, because trust is the product. Every number carries a provenance mark. Numbers read from the photo or email are solid and link back to the evidence: tap one and the source crop or quote lights up. Assumed numbers are dotted and labeled "my guess, drag me". There are no unsourced conversions like "41 hours waiting" unless the person sets the inputs themselves.

3) Use roughly 8 archetypes instead of a generic engine. Claude chooses and fills one of a small, well-designed set: rate times time (subscriptions and delivery), spoil-by timeline (fridge and pantry), cost-per-use (closet, gym, tools), bill-vs-dial (utilities), countdown-with-scenario (leases, return windows), reorder point (shop stock and pills), budget-split, and space mission (pins, timer, before/after). Each archetype has a hand-built, beautiful renderer and a safe evaluator limited to whitelisted operations. That gives 8 deep instruments rather than infinite shallow ones, and it is buildable by 5 people.

4) Make the hinge glow. Each instrument highlights the one variable that actually changes the outcome, and the commit button sits on that hinge. Committing produces exactly one prepared action: a draft (never auto-sent), an .ics or Drive file, or a timed photo mission.

5) Make the return loop the hook. The home screen is the Bench, a wall of your instruments, each showing a small ghost line: where you said you'd be versus where you are. On reopen a "Since last time" line greets you, for example: "Delivery: 2x this week, on track. Fridge: you cooked the spinach. Gym: no new receipts, check in?" A new photo or new mail snaps onto the existing instrument automatically.

6) Give it a humane ending and a real stopping cue. A session is "tune one, commit one, verify one". After that the screen says "Bench is set." and shows the running total of commitments kept, framed as dollars and spaces actually changed. It never shows a streak.

7) Use social features sparingly. Room mode lets a partner or roommate scrub the same household instrument, such as the shared grocery bill, live together. Downloads let you share one instrument as a self-contained HTML explorable, and that becomes the viral artifact.

8) Build a demo bench for use outside Claude, with three pre-baked instruments (receipt, fridge, subscription), so the magic shows even with no AI available.

Build split: (1) capture and the forge prompt, with archetype choice, JSON validation and a re-ask on bad JSON; (2) the safe evaluator plus the provenance model; (3) the scrubbable-prose and chart renderers for the 8 archetypes; (4) the Bench wall, db, ghost lines and the since-last-time summary; (5) the action layer: drafts, files, .ics, and the photo-mission timer with before/after verification.
  Ranking: H3 > H5 > I7 > I11 > H2 > H4 > H1 > I13

Victor: Build H3, "Workbench". It is the only finalist that is a new medium and not a new costume. It is also the only one that answers all four of the panel's sharpest objections at once.

1. It is not the inbox-triage app. Eight of the fifteen pitches, and four of these finalists (H1, H2, H4 and, underneath the tiles, I13), come down to "an agent hands you a pre-chewed draft and you approve it." That is the passive posture of the feed, with consent added. The person still cannot see inside the decision or steer it. In Workbench the interaction is thinking with your thumb. You grab the [6] in "You pay $87/mo across [6] subscriptions" and drag it to 3. The yearly total, the bar chart and the three cancellation drafts lined up beside it all reflow while your finger is still moving. Reading the tool, steering it and acting on it are the same gesture. Nobody has shipped that on a phone, and it has only become possible this year, because Claude can now write a model of your own world in four seconds.

2. It does not depend on Gmail quality. The camera is the main source of supply and the inbox is a bonus. A receipt, the fridge, a utility bill, a closet or a pill bottle each becomes an instrument. This user's shop-heavy inbox (orders, suppliers) turns out to be good material for instruments: margins, reorder points, cost per order. It is poor material for "Maya, 214 days ago" cards. H1, H2 and H4 bet their first session on finding a friend in that inbox. Workbench bets it on one photo.

3. It can fill the couch-and-thumb moment honestly. A queue runs dry in three minutes. A model you can explore does not: you can keep scrubbing assumptions, comparing futures and finding the hinge for as long as you are curious, and that time is spent thinking about your own life. I11's fatal flaw is the reverse problem. It is healthy, but it needs you to stand up, so it can't replace the 11pm scroll. You can tidy a nightstand only so often.

4. It has a return loop that isn't "more email arrived". This is the ghost line. You commit to a future, and the next photo of the same kind of thing snaps onto the model and shows the gap between where you said you'd be and where you are. That is the most humane hook in the field: it is about reality, not streaks.

Against the rest:
- I7 is the soul of Workbench, but on its own it has no hands. You scrub, you feel clever, and nothing changes in your life. That is the "toy of false precision" charge. H3 adds the action layer and the hinge.
- I13 and H5 dress the dashboard up. A desktop of tiles is where attention goes to die. Fusion is a demo trick, and melting tiles is housekeeping. H5 is basically H3 plus Kiln's desktop shell, which makes it a fifth subsystem bolted on. It splits the build across forging animation, fusion and the desktop, when the effort should go into making one instrument feel inevitable. It is buildable, but the effort goes to the wrong place.
- I11 is the most honest pitch, and it lives on inside Workbench as an action type: an instrument can end in a 7-minute photo mission with a verified before/after. As a whole app, though, it is four small apps that each need you to stand up.
- H1, H2 and H4 are the same machine three times: one prepared card at a time, held to commit, then the app ends. They are ethical and well made, but they stay inside Gmail, and relief is not desire. All three lean on I11 to stay alive, which shows that the core does not hold up without it. H2's ledger and H4's garden are metaphors laid over a list.

The real risks in Workbench are false precision and a fragile generic renderer. Both can be fixed in the design, which I set out in the improvements.
  Improvements: To make Workbench groundbreaking, irresistible and humane, build it this way.

1. Honest numbers. Every number on screen has a visible origin, and the origin decides how it looks.
- SEEN: read from your photo or email. Underlined in solid ink. Tapping it flashes the exact crop of the receipt or email it came from.
- ASSUMED: a guess you can drag. Dotted underline, and it always starts as an editable guess, never a claim.
- DERIVED: computed locally from the other numbers. Plain text, and tapping it reveals the formula as a tiny data-flow strip.
Ranges render as uncertainty bands, not single lines. A model can never present an assumption as a fact. This answers the "41 hours waiting" objection.

2. A small, fixed vocabulary instead of a generic renderer. Claude writes a JSON model using only these:
- variables with min, max, step, unit and origin
- formulas in a whitelisted expression language, evaluated in a sandbox (about 150 lines, no eval)
- one template sentence with bound slots
- exactly one of four charts: timeline, cost-over-time, stacked bar or threshold gauge
- a list of actions

The page validates the JSON and asks Claude again if it fails. Hand-tune six "golden" instrument kinds (receipt or subscription, fridge spoil-by, utility bill, closet cost-per-wear, shop margin and reorder, plant or medication schedule) so that the first session is precise and correct. Claude chooses a kind and fills it in; anything else falls back to the generic grammar.

3. The hinge, computed rather than claimed. The page runs a local sensitivity sweep and makes the one variable that most changes the outcome glow. A sentence states it: "Everything depends on this one: visits per month."

4. Commit means act. Dragging past a threshold reveals the real action inline: a Gmail draft (never sent), a Drive sheet, an .ics reminder, or a 7-minute photo mission with pins and a before/after wipe verified by a second photo. Holding to commit pins the setting as an intention.

5. The ghost line as the only score. A new photo or new email of the same kind snaps onto the existing instrument. A dotted line shows the committed future, a solid line shows reality, and the shaded gap between them shows your progress. On reopen, "Since last time" lists only real deltas.

6. The Bench, where browsing is the addictive part. The wall of instruments is something to explore, not a feed. Swipe between your instruments, and each one is a live miniature you can scrub right on the wall. An empty wall offers three suggested photos ("your last receipt", "inside your fridge", "a bill"), so activation needs nothing but the camera.

7. Room mode. A partner or roommate drags the same household instruments live, and you can see both people's fingers on the numbers as you argue about the future together.

8. A natural end. Once intentions are set, the screen dims to "Bench is quiet. 3 futures committed." It has no streaks and no fake rewards.

9. Demo mode. Ship three pre-forged golden instruments so the app is magical even outside Claude.

Build split for the five builders:
- (1) capture plus the agentic forge over images, Gmail and Drive, with schema validation and re-asking
- (2) the expression sandbox, the origin model and the sensitivity or hinge engine
- (3) scrubbable prose plus the four live charts at 60fps under touch
- (4) the Bench wall, db persistence, ghost-line snapping and "since last time"
- (5) the action layer: drafts, files, .ics, photo missions with before/after verification, and room co-scrubbing
  Ranking: H3 > I7 > H5 > I11 > H4 > H1 > H2 > I13

Raskin: Build H3, Workbench, but rebuilt camera-first and held to honesty. I helped build the infinite feed, and I know what it exploits: a thumb with nothing to do and a mind with nothing to decide. TikTok wins because it never asks anything of you. Every concept that answers it with "a smaller queue of chores" will lose. Relief is not desire, and nobody hold-to-commits a dentist reply at 11pm for pleasure. Every concept that answers it with "more novelty" (Kiln's surprise tiles) just rebuilds the variable-reward slot machine with a nicer conscience. Workbench is the only finalist with a pull I can defend: agency. You point at a piece of your real life, it becomes an instrument, and your finger bends your own future while you watch. That is compelling the way a musical instrument is compelling, not the way a slot machine is. It ends in a real act in the world: a 7-minute pinned mission, a draft, a file. Then it brings you back with the most humane re-engagement hook anyone proposed, the ghost line: "you said 1x a week, reality says 2x." That is a mirror, not a notification.

Why the others lose:
- I11 One Square Meter (my own pitch) is the healthiest thing here, and I'm ranking it second, not first. It is an AI cleaning coach. You can only tidy a nightstand so often, and it answers "something I could never have imagined" with "something I've imagined." It should be the action layer of Workbench, not the whole product.
- I7 Underlay is the right primitive, but it has no hand. You scrub, you nod, nothing in your life changes, and by the third receipt it's a party trick. Its false precision ("41 hours waiting") is also a quiet dark pattern: confident numbers manipulate.
- H1 Clearing, H2 Dividend and H4 Tend are the same inbox-triage app in three skins. They bet the first session on an untested Gmail. This user's address looks like a shop account, so that inbox is likely orders and suppliers, not "Maya, 214 days ago." They also fill 3 minutes and then run dry. H4 is the most humane of the three and H2 has the best metric, but a capped deck of chores does not displace an hour of TikTok. It displaces nothing.
- H5 is Workbench plus fusion, melting, embers and a desktop, which is everything the panel called a party trick, and it's unbuildable in one sitting.
- I13 Kiln is a dashboard that runs on surprise. Dashboards are where attention goes to die, and "what did it forge today?" is variable reward with no stopping cue.

Workbench has fatal flaws too: a fully generic renderer produces shallow calculators, and Gmail-first forging inherits the thin-inbox risk. Both are fixable, and the improvements below fix them. The others' flaws are their premise.
  Improvements: 1) Camera-first, Gmail second. The first 30 seconds never touch the inbox: one photo (fridge, receipt, closet, bill, a messy corner, a plant) gives a magic moment guaranteed on any account. Gmail and Drive are an optional second lens ("also look for this in my mail"), used to deepen an instrument, e.g. finding all 6 subscription receipts once you've photographed one.
2) Do not build a generic model renderer. Hand-craft about 6 instrument archetypes that each feel inevitable: Spoil Clock (fridge: what turns when, cook order tonight), Leak (recurring spend from receipts and subscriptions), Cost-per-Use (closet, gym, gadgets), Bill Dial (utility or thermostat), Square Meter (physical chaos: pins plus a timer), Living Thing (plant or pet care curve). Claude classifies the photo and fills that archetype's typed schema with values, pins at normalized x/y on the photo, and a template sentence. The page computes everything locally with fixed formulas per archetype, so there's no eval sandbox and no fragile generic schema. Quality comes from design, not luck.
3) Honest numbers as a visible design element. Every draggable number has a provenance mark: solid if it was read from the photo or your mail (tap it to see the glowing crop or the email line), dotted if it's an assumption you set. Show ranges, not false precision. Each instrument has one hinge, a glowing number labeled "this is the one that decides it."
4) Steering ends in the world. Committing to a setting produces one prepared real act: a 7-minute pinned mission with a timer screen that has nothing to scroll, a Gmail draft (never auto-sent), a Drive sheet, or an .ics reminder. The after-photo verifies the result with a before/after wipe, and that wipe is the payoff.
5) The ghost line is the only reason to return. On reopen you see a quiet "since last time" strip ("Fridge: you planned zero waste, two items spoiled. Leak: $38 cancelled, still holding.") and a nudge to photograph the same thing again so reality snaps onto your committed line. No streaks, no XP, no chests, no infinite wall.
6) Designed stopping cue: one instrument steered plus one act committed makes a complete session. The bench "sets" and says "Done. You changed one real thing." Then it actually stops showing anything new.
7) One metric across everything: "Steered," the real-world delta you committed to and then verified (dollars kept, food saved, square meters reclaimed).
8) Optional room mode: a partner or roommate sees your live mission and reveal. Social pull from witnesses, not likes.
9) Five-way build split: (a) photo intake, archetype classification and vision JSON with pins, retrying on invalid output; (b) the 6 archetype engines with local formulas, provenance and the hinge; (c) the scrubbable-prose, pins-on-photo and mini-chart renderer, with gestures; (d) the action layer (mission timer, before/after wipe, Gmail drafts, Drive and .ics); (e) the bench wall, db persistence, ghost lines, "since last time", room, and a full demo mode for use outside Claude.
  Ranking: H3 > I11 > I7 > H4 > H2 > H5 > H1 > I13

Lu: Build H3, "Workbench". I'm also folding in the two things from H5 that are worth keeping and dropping the rest of H5's extra layers.

Here is the test the brief sets: "something I could never have imagined." Only one thing has become possible in the last year. A frontier model can look at a piece of your own world and build working software about it on the spot, software you can hold and steer with your thumb. Workbench is the only finalist built entirely on that. The others use Claude as a very good autocomplete for emails, or as a cleaning coach.

Against the card-deck hybrids (H1 Clearing, H2 Dividend, H4 Tend). These are one product in three costumes. Each is a queue of pre-chewed outputs that you approve or defer: hold to commit, swipe to defer. That is the passive, consume-the-feed posture the brief is trying to escape, now with chores in it. Relief is not desire, so nobody reaches for a chore deck at 11pm. All three also put the first session at the mercy of an inbox nobody has tested. This user's address is a shop account. Their Gmail is probably suppliers, orders and newsletters, not "Maya, 14 months ago." So the People suit's magic moment may never happen, and the first card could misread a supplier as a friend. Bolting on the photo mission to fix supply turns them into three apps in one deck. Their honest ending is admirable, but it ends after three minutes of approving things, and that is not a replacement for an hour of thumb time. H2 at least has a single metric (the Dividend), which is why it ranks highest of the three.

Against I11 "One Square Meter". It is the most robust activation in the field and it gets you off the couch. But by week two you have tidied the nightstand and there is nothing new to find. It is a coach, not a medium. Vision cleaning advice is also the obvious use of the model. It should not be the product. It should become one action inside Workbench: an instrument you commit to can produce a pinned 7-minute mission.

Against I13 "Kiln" (my own pitch, which I'm demoting). The panel is right. Eight widget primitives produce "Packages (4)", which is a list wearing a costume, and a desktop of tiles is a dashboard where attention goes to die. Fusing tiles is a demo trick. Kiln's real idea was software forged from your life. It only becomes groundbreaking when what gets forged is alive, meaning scrubbable and causal, rather than a static widget.

Against I7 "Underlay". This is the best primitive in the field, and Workbench is built on it. On its own it has two cracks. First, false precision: "41 hours waiting" is made-up arithmetic presented as fact. Second, it stops at insight. You scrub, you nod, nothing changes in your life. H3 fixes the second crack by making the committed number turn into a real action.

Against H5. It is H3 with every mechanic stacked on top: fuse, melt, a desktop, embers, intentions, ghost lines and a session ending. Five builders can't polish all of that in one sitting, and the panel already named fusion as the weakest part. I'm keeping two things from H5: negative preferences from melting a tool, and the "Kiln cooled" ending. Everything else in H5 is scope that would dilute the polish.

Why Workbench wins:
1. It is the only finalist where reading, steering and acting are a single gesture. You drag the 6 subscriptions down to 3, and the three cancellation drafts get written beside your thumb while it is still moving.
2. Its supply never runs out and doesn't depend on Gmail. Every receipt, bill, fridge, closet, pill bottle or label is a new instrument, so a thin inbox is fine.
3. It gives you a real reason to come back that isn't "more email arrived." The ghost line asks whether reality followed the future you committed to. You find out by taking the next photo.
4. Every tool it builds is unique to your life. That is the "unlike anything else" the brief asks for, and it is earned by computation rather than by a new skin.
5. It is humane. Exploring has no feed to fall into. The thing that hooks you is watching your own future bend under your finger, and every session ends in a real action or a deliberate stop.
  Improvements: 1. Camera first, inbox second. The first session must never wait on Gmail. Open it and the screen says "Show me anything you paid for, own, or have to deal with." Take the photo and the instrument is live within about 5 seconds. Gmail and Drive come in only as enrichment for an instrument that already exists. For example, on a gym receipt it asks "Want me to check how often you actually went?" This removes the thin-inbox and spinner-first problems, and it also handles the case where this is a shop inbox. A shop inbox is actually an advantage: supplier invoices make excellent instruments.

2. Truth labels on every number. This is what kills false precision. Every draggable number shows where it came from, as one of three visibly different kinds:
   - Observed: a solid underline, and tapping it shows the crop of your photo or the email line it came from.
   - Inferred: a dotted underline, with Claude's reason in one line.
   - Assumed: a hollow chip, glowing as an invitation to set it yourself.
   The instrument says how sure it is, and you raise its accuracy by turning Assumed numbers into Observed ones, either with another photo or with an inbox check. Getting a number closer to the truth becomes the game, which is a better hook than XP and honest by construction.

3. Molds, not a free-form schema. Claude doesn't invent arbitrary models. It chooses one of about six tested instrument molds and fills in its parameters:
   - Recurring cost (subscriptions, delivery habit, gym)
   - Decay clock (fridge, plants, return windows, prescriptions)
   - Cost per use (closet, gear)
   - Budget split (bill, receipt)
   - Countdown with a scenario (lease, warranty, renewal)
   - Physical reset (a cluttered corner, which leads to a pinned mission and a before/after reveal)
   Each mold has a renderer we hand-polish, plus a small safe expression evaluator. That keeps the build reliable for 5 people working in one sitting and means every instrument looks made, not generated. Claude's job is the parts only it can do: reading the photo, writing the sentence, and spotting the hinge.

4. One glowing hinge per instrument. It is the single number that decides the answer. The first touch always lands on it, so within 2 seconds the person learns that this sentence is alive.

5. Commit turns into a real act every time. Releasing on a value produces one of four things:
   - a Gmail draft (never sent automatically)
   - a Drive file
   - an .ics reminder for the moment the ghost line should be checked
   - a 7-minute pinned photo mission
   The intention is saved with a target number.

6. The ghost line as the return loop. The next photo of the same kind of thing snaps onto the existing instrument. Your committed future appears as a ghost curve, your actual position as a solid point, and the gap is the only score. There are no streaks. On return the screen says "Since last time: fridge waste $23 → $6. Gym: still 2 visits." in one line.

7. The bench is a wall, not a desktop. Instruments sit like specimens in a cabinet, and each one breathes slightly when its ghost line is due. You can melt an instrument (from H5), and Claude learns what you don't care about. There is no fusion.

8. A designed ending. Once a session's instruments have been scrubbed and committed, the bench dims: "Bench cooled. 2 instruments built, 1 future committed, $412/yr in play." If you want more, it offers one more photo, never one more scroll.

9. Build split, five pieces:
   (1) Capture, the vision-to-mold prompt with JSON validation and a retry on bad output, and an optional Gmail/Drive enrichment loop.
   (2) The mold library and safe evaluator.
   (3) The scrubbable-prose renderer with truth labels and the hinge glow, plus mini charts and ghost curves.
   (4) The action layer: confirmation sheets, drafts, Drive files, .ics, and the pinned photo mission with before/after verification.
   (5) The bench wall, db persistence, intentions and ghost-line history, melted preferences, and a fully worked demo bench for use outside Claude.
  Ranking: H3 > H5 > I7 > I11 > H2 > H4 > H1 > I13
